title: Theology is not a science by Aristotle's strict definition, yet it is rightly called science by the evidence of the consequence

pass_b_english: So much, then, is clear about the necessity of theology. But now, that we may hold clearly and distinctly what it is, we must first inquire into its genus. The first question, therefore, is whether our theology is a science. On which we say that theology is not a science accurately speaking, and according to the definition of science laid down by Aristotle. For science according to Aristotle is an evident assent: but theological conclusions are not evident. And that is because they are gathered from inevident principles. For faith is the habit of the theological principles. But faith is an inevident habit. For the Apostle opposes faith to sight: ([[2 Corinthians 5:7 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 5:7]]) — By faith, he says, we walk, not by sight. And ([[Hebrews 11:1 >> Bible:Hebrews 11:1]]) teaches that faith is of things that are not seen. Faith, he says, is the substance of things hoped for, and the argument of things that are not seen.

Now those things are said to be evident which of themselves move the intellect to the knowledge of them — that is, which of themselves persuade and commend themselves to the mind, and by their own light so strike and convince the mind that it cannot but assent to them. That this does not suit the mysteries of our faith is plain. For they are not things known of themselves, whose truth of itself lays itself open to our mind. But that we assent to them, we do because of the authority and testimony of God, who revealed and confirmed them by his Word.

But here a distinction must be made between the evidence of the consequent and the evidence of the consequence. For theological conclusions are indeed not evident: yet the consequence by which they are drawn from their principles is evident. From inevident premises, to be sure — but they are gathered evidently. For example: that Christ is true God and true man is a principle of faith, which of itself is not evident, but is believed because of God's testimony alone. Yet from it it evidently follows that in Christ there are two wills, one divine and the other human. And so in this respect theology lacks nothing toward the true character of a science.

Although, however, theology is not a science properly and strictly speaking, and according to all the conditions of science laid down by Aristotle, still there is no habit of the mind to which it more nearly approaches, and to which it ought rather to be referred. For it is a certain knowledge evidently deduced from certain principles, which, though they are inevident, are no less certain than if they were evident. And so it is rightly and fittingly called a science, nor can it be designated by any more apt name.
source_text:
XII. Sic ergo de Theologiae necessitate patet. Jam vero ut quid ea sit, clare et distincte teneamus, primo in genus ejus inquirendum est. Quaeritur ergo primo an Theologia nostra sit scientia. Super qua re dicimus Theologiam scientiam non esse accurate loquendo, et juxta definitionem scientiae ab Aristotele positam. Etenim scientia secundum Aristotelem est assensus evidens: Atqui conclusiones Theologicae non sunt evidentes. Et hoc quia colliguntur ex principiis inevidentibus. Fides enim est habitus principiorum Theologicorum. Atqui fides est habitus inevidens. Nam Apostolus fidem opponit aspectui: 2 Corinth. 5. Per fidem, inquit, ambulamus non per aspectum. Et Hebr. 11. docet fidem eorum esse quae non videntur. Fides, inquit, est rerum quae sperantur substantia, et eorum quae non videntur argumentum.

XIII. Illa autem dicuntur esse evidentia, quae per se intellectum movent ad sui cognitionem, id est, quae seipsa menti suadent et commendant, et luce sua mentem ita feriunt et convincunt, ut non possit non iis assentiri. Quod fidei nostrae mysteriis non convenire palam est. Non sunt enim res per se notae, quarumque veritas ex se menti nostrae se prodat. Sed quod illis assentimur, id facimus propter authoritatem et testimonium Dei, qui ea Verbo suo revelavit et confirmavit.

XIV. Verum hic est distinguendum inter evidentiam consequentis et consequentiae. Conclusiones enim Theologicae non sunt quidem evidentes: sed consequentia tamen, qua ex principiis suis deducuntur, evidens est. Ex praemissis quidem inevidentibus: sed evidenter colliguntur. Exempli causa, Christum esse verum Deum et verum hominem, fidei principium est, quod ex se non est evidens, sed propter solum Dei testimonium creditur. At inde tamen evidenter sequitur in Christo duas esse voluntates, divinam unam et alteram humanam. Ideoque hac in parte Theologiae nihil deest ad veram scientiae rationem.

XV. Licet autem Theologia scientia non sit proprie et stricte loquendo, et juxta scientiae conditiones omnes ab Aristotele positas, nullus tamen est habitus mentis ad quem magis accedat, et ad quem potius debeat revocari. Est enim cognitio certa evidenter deducta ex principiis certis, quae, licet inevidentia sint, non minus tamen certa sunt, quam si essent evidentia. Ideoque recte et convenienter scientia dicitur, nec alio aptiori nomine designari potest.
